name: bluewater-shorts-23-32
lines: She got two quotes for the same job. She picked the one that cost more.
Not because she likes spending money.
The first guy walked in, measured, and talked about himself for twenty minutes.
The second guy asked three questions before he said a single number.
What's bothering you most about it? What happened the last time you had it fixed? When do you need it done by?
Then his quote answered all three.
She didn't buy the cheaper job. She bought the guy who listened.
At your next estimate, ask those three before you touch your tape measure.
How much for a new furnace?
It depends. I'd have to come out and take a look.
Click. She's already calling the next number.
You weren't wrong. It does depend. But she didn't ask for a contract. She asked if she can afford you.
So give her a range. Most of ours land between this and this. It moves with the size of the house and what's already there.
Now she knows you're real, and she knows roughly what's coming.
Tonight, write your three most common jobs on a card. Put an honest range beside each one.
The job's done. The invoice is paid. The truck's packed.
For most companies, that's the end of the story.
Tomorrow at ten, send one text.
Hi, it's me from yesterday. How's the new tap holding up?
That's it. No sale. No ask.
If something's wrong, you hear it from her before the whole internet does.
If everything's perfect, she just found out you're the one who checks.
Guess whose name she says when her sister needs a plumber.
One text. The day after. Every job.
Your customer is watching you through her front window.
You haven't knocked yet. She's already deciding.
A coffee cup on the dash. A hoodie with paint on it. Boots headed for her white carpet.
None of that says you do bad work. All of it says something.
So fix the first ten seconds.
A clean shirt with your name on it. Boot covers in your back pocket. And say your name before you say anything else.
It costs less than a tank of gas. And now you look like the price you're about to quote.
Last night, somebody in your town's Facebook group asked for a good electrician.
Forty one people answered.
Nobody said your name.
Here's the thing. Those forty one weren't experts. Each one was just a happy customer that somebody remembered to ask.
So at the end of your next good job, ask for one small favour.
If anyone in the group ever asks for an electrician, would you say my name?
One sentence. Most people are glad to.
You can't post your way into that thread. Your customers can walk you in.
It's four o'clock on a Tuesday. You're open. Your truck is running.
Google says you're closed.
Somebody changed your hours two years ago. Maybe it was you. Nobody's looked since.
So right now, a customer with a real problem is looking at a red word beside your name.
She doesn't call to check. She calls the one that says open.
Tonight, search your own business name and look at three things.
Your hours. Your holiday hours. And the area you say you cover.
It takes five minutes, and it's free.
You drove forty minutes across town to look at a dripping tap.
You looked at it for ninety seconds. You gave a price. They said they'd think about it.
Forty minutes back.
Stop doing that.
When they call, say this. Can you text me a photo of it?
Now you can give them a real range in two minutes, from your truck.
The ones who were only shopping drop off. The serious ones book the visit.
And put it on your voicemail. For a faster quote, text a photo to this number.
The best salesman for your plumbing business is an electrician.
Think about it. He's in the same houses you want. He sees the old pipes while he's fixing the panel.
And every week somebody asks him, do you know a good plumber?
Right now, he shrugs.
So pick two trades that work in the same homes as you. Not competitors. Neighbours.
Buy each one a coffee. Trade numbers. Then send them a job first.
Don't ask for anything back. Just send one.
People remember who sent them work.
One price on a quote is a yes or no question.
And when people aren't sure, they say no. Or they say nothing.
Three prices is a different question. Which one?
So on your next quote, give three.
The basic fix for today's problem. The one you'd put in your own house. And the one that means they never call you about this again.
A lot of people skip the cheapest once they can see what it leaves out.
You didn't push anybody. You let them choose.
In ten minutes, a stranger is going to knock on your customer's door.
She's home alone. She doesn't know his name. She doesn't know his face.
All she knows is that somebody from your company is coming between noon and four.
Now picture this instead.
Her phone buzzes. Hi, it's Dev from your plumbing company. I'm twenty minutes away. And there's his photo.
When she opens the door, she already knows who's standing there.
One text from the truck. Ten seconds.
And it's the kind of thing people tell their neighbours about.
